title: Simulated Global Radar — 3-km Storm Forecast
abstract: A worldwide storm forecast fine enough to show individual thunderstorms. The colours are the ones you already know from a weather radar map: blues and greens for light precipitation, yellows and oranges for heavy rain, reds and magentas for the most intense cores. Hover anywhere to read the value in dBZ — the decibel scale radar meteorologists use for how strongly precipitation reflects a radar beam. Nothing here was measured by an actual radar. The field is what a radar *would* see if one were parked at that spot, computed by a model whose grid cells are about 3 km across — small enough that it builds each storm explicitly instead of estimating them statistically the way coarser global models must. That is the difference you are looking at: squall lines with structure, hurricane eyewalls, afternoon storms firing over land and dying after dark, everywhere on Earth at once rather than only where a radar network happens to exist.
attribution_text: Experimental 3-km global forecast produced with the Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) by the NSF National Center for Atmospheric Research, Mesoscale and Microscale Meteorology Laboratory, on the NSF NCAR-Wyoming Supercomputing Center's Derecho system.
